The status host is a property no configuration of the set defines (billing's application.yml sets only the accounting lookup, legacy and SFTP addresses), and the region comes from an environment variable; nothing shows it is one of the internal units.

The outbox rows are written with the exchange fleet.workorder.events and the keys workorder.created, workorder.<id>.completed, workorder.<id>.cancelled and maintenance.reminder; notification-service binds all four, and work-order's own read-model queue binds workorder.created.

risks.how: Both services build an HMAC JWT decoder from the same shared-secret property, defaulted to a placeholder value in config.

risks.reference: PartnerStatusClient is a component that resolves `accounting.status-host` and `accounting.status-api-version` in its constructor; no configuration in the set defines them, so billing fails to start unless an outside source supplies them.
risks.how: The component's constructor needs two properties that no configuration file of the set defines, so the context fails to start without an outside value.

risks.reference: The customer portal allows credentialed cross-origin requests to `/graphql` from any origin, applies that rule in its security chain, exempts `/graphql` from CSRF protection and sends its session cookie with SameSite=None, so another website can run portal queries and mutations as the signed-in customer.
risks.how: The /graphql CORS mapping allows the origin pattern * with credentials.

risks.reference: The staging overlay starts notification-service with the staging profile, whose `ddl-auto: create-drop` drops its tables at shutdown, so delivery records are lost on every restart.
risks.how: Staging activates a profile whose Hibernate setting creates the schema at start and drops it at shutdown.

risks.reference: The billing production profile, which the billing image always runs, holds the live PayGrid request-signing key as a literal; it signs every charge and refund request.
risks.how: A literal key in the profile every deployed billing runs, used to sign outgoing PayGrid requests.

risks.reference: Work-order (Commons 2.1.0) sends `VehicleReleased` with `accountId`; notification bundles Commons 1.9.4, where the field is `customerId`, so it reads no customer and cannot send the pickup notice.
risks.how: The shared message type renamed a field between the Commons versions the sender and the receiver bundle.

risks.reference: The staff Angular environment holds `http://localhost:8088/api` and `ws://localhost:8088`, and its image runs a plain `npm run build` with no file replacement, so outside the Compose host every API and STOMP call goes to the user's own machine.
risks.how: The environment file the build bakes in holds localhost addresses and nothing replaces them.

risks.reference: Billing asks PayGrid to refund inside the transaction before it parses the state and records the refund; if that parse, the insert or the commit fails, the refund is made but not recorded.
risks.how: The provider call precedes the local writes in one transaction.

risks.reference: Parts inventory places the PartsHub replenishment order inside its transaction with a fresh random request id; if the transaction rolls back, the supplier holds an order FleetCare has no record of.
risks.how: The supplier call precedes the commit, with a request id that changes on each attempt.

risks.reference: Notification keeps STOMP subscriptions in an in-memory simple broker while its listeners share durable queues; with two replicas each event reaches only the dispatchers connected to the instance that consumed it.
risks.how: An in-memory STOMP broker behind queues that several replicas share.

risks.reference: POST /api/payments has no role check and billing never enables method security, so any signed-in user can pay any invoice and billing's `@PreAuthorize` checks do not run.
risks.how: No role annotation and no method security in the service.

risks.reference: The work-order endpoint that requests a vehicle diagnostic snapshot has no role check and the chain only requires sign-in, so any signed-in user can put snapshot requests for any vehicle on the vehicle command topic.
risks.how: No role annotation on a command endpoint; the chain only requires sign-in.

risks.reference: The vehicle maintenance endpoint creates a work order for the customer id the body names with no role check, so any signed-in user can open work orders for any customer.
risks.how: No role annotation on an endpoint that creates work orders for a body-named customer.

decoys.looksLike: Technician-service trusts role values for @PreAuthorize checks that might come from a request.
decoys.safeBecause: Roles are read from the realm_access claim of a JWT validated by oauth2ResourceServer and every exchange except health requires authentication; no identity header is read.

decoys.looksLike: Database passwords appear in service configuration, like a hardcoded secret.
decoys.safeBecause: They are bare environment placeholders with no default value, so no secret is in the code.

decoys.looksLike: Work-order service has JPA and a database but may let Hibernate manage the schema.
decoys.safeBecause: ddl-auto is validate and Flyway is enabled, so schema changes come only from migrations.

decoys.looksLike: A CORS policy lets every origin call parts inventory.
decoys.safeBecause: The open policy covers one GET that returns only whether a part number is in stock, without credentials; nothing private or state-changing is reachable from another origin.

decoys.looksLike: Notification lets Hibernate update its schema.
decoys.safeBecause: ddl-auto update is only the default: the image always starts with the prod profile (validate), and the staging overlay switches to staging. Only the developer Compose override, whose local profile has no file of its own, falls back to update, against a throwaway local database, so no deployed data is at risk.

decoys.looksLike: Technician-service takes the caller's tenant from a request header.
decoys.safeBecause: The roster export reads X-Tenant-Id but refuses the request with 403 unless it equals the tenant_id claim of the validated token, so a caller cannot choose another tenant.

decoys.looksLike: The portal calls a technician path that no technician controller declares.
decoys.safeBecause: technician-service serves the path with a functional route that streams availability events, and the portal reads it as an event stream and takes the first event.

decoys.looksLike: A PayGrid API key is committed in billing's configuration.
decoys.safeBecause: The literal key sits in the local profile, which only the developer Compose override activates, and points at the local PayGrid mock; every deployed run takes the key only from PAYGRID_API_KEY.

decoys.looksLike: Work-order keeps STOMP subscriptions in each instance's memory while it runs two instances.
decoys.safeBecause: Each work-order instance binds its own temporary queue to a fanout exchange and relays every bay change to its local simple broker, so a board connected to any instance gets every change.

decoys.looksLike: VehicleReceived is passed between units that bundle different Commons versions.
decoys.safeBecause: VehicleReceived has the same fields in Commons 1.9.4 and 2.1.0, so notification reads what work-order sends.

decoys.looksLike: The yard board's environment file points at localhost.
decoys.safeBecause: environment.ts holds localhost, but the app overwrites it at start from runtime-config.json, which the image's entrypoint script writes at every container start (default /api).

decoys.looksLike: Work-order lets callers read the workshop bay board without signing in.
decoys.safeBecause: The board is a workshop display: the open GET returns only bay names and states, nothing about customers or vehicles, and the open STOMP endpoint accepts only the workshop's own origin and carries the same bay states.

investigate.why: The staff app calls GET /api/staff/operations/summary; the gateway's routes cover only customer and work-order paths, so the call reaches no service.
technician-service serves the path with a functional route that streams availability events, and the portal reads it as an event stream and takes the first event.
The gateway's fleet overview calls /api/technicians/{id}/skils; technician-service serves /skills, so the call gets no endpoint.

The Feign client sends GET to the reschedule path, which technician-service serves only as POST; scheduling calls it when the appointment starts after the known shift ends, so that scheduling fails with 405.
environment.ts sets apiBaseUrl to http://localhost:8088/api; angular.json has no file replacement and the staff image runs a plain npm run build, so the deployed app calls localhost.
environment.ts sets webSocketBaseUrl to ws://localhost:8088 and the event client connects to it; no build replaces the file, and the staff image runs a plain npm run build.
environment.ts holds localhost, but the app overwrites it at start from runtime-config.json, which the image's entrypoint script writes at every container start (default /api).
The roster export reads X-Tenant-Id but refuses the request with 403 unless it equals the tenant_id claim of the validated token, so a caller cannot choose another tenant.

Work-order binds X-Roles with getHeader, the first value, and the gateway adds its own value with headers.add instead of replacing a client-sent copy. The priority endpoint checks only that forwarded role, so any signed-in user who sends X-Roles: DISPATCHER can change a work order's priority.

Work-order binds X-User-Id with getHeader, the first value, and the gateway adds rather than replaces it; the priority endpoint records that forwarded user ID as who made the change, so a caller can record changes under another user's name.

The portal's /graphql mapping allows every origin pattern with credentials, its security chain applies those CORS rules and exempts /graphql from CSRF, and its session cookie is SameSite=None, so any website a signed-in customer visits can run GraphQL queries and mutations as that customer.
The open policy covers one GET that returns only whether a part number is in stock, without credentials; nothing private or state-changing is reachable from another origin.

pay charges PayGrid (line 38) before it inserts the payment and updates the invoice, and throws if the invoice changed meanwhile (44-45); the rollback leaves a charge with no payment record.

refund asks PayGrid to refund inside the transaction before it records the refund; when parseStatus rejects the provider's state, or the insert or commit fails, the refund is made but not recorded, and amountReserved no longer counts it, so a new request can refund again.
pay is @Transactional and publishes to RabbitMQ and JMS before it returns, so consumers can see a payment the transaction later rolls back.
catalogItem is a GET that reads the supplier's catalogue; nothing at the supplier changes, so sending it before the commit has no effect anyone can act on.

reorderIfNeeded places the supplier order inside the transaction with a fresh random request id; if the transaction then rolls back (parseExpectedAt throws on a bad timestamp), the local order is gone and the next run orders again under a new id.

The alert listener sends the diagnostic command to Kafka before it saves the work order in its transaction, but the command asks the vehicle for a snapshot and needs none of that data; a rollback only means the redelivered alert asks again.
getShift is a GET that reads a technician's shift to check availability; it changes nothing in technician-service, so nothing can act on uncommitted data.

notification-service uses Spring's in-memory simple broker and production runs two replicas, so a push sent on one replica never reaches clients connected to the other.
Each work-order instance binds its own temporary queue to a fanout exchange and relays every bay change to its local simple broker, so a board connected to any instance gets every change.
POST /api/payments has no role check, and billing never enables method security (no @EnableMethodSecurity), so any authenticated caller can charge any invoice.
POST /api/payments/{id}/reconcile only reads the payment and returns a fixed 'queued' answer; it changes nothing, so the missing role check lets no caller do more than read.

POST /api/vehicles/{vin}/diagnostics has no role check, and the security chain only requires sign-in for it, so any signed-in user can put snapshot requests for any vehicle on the vehicle command topic.
POST /api/vehicles/{vin}/maintenance creates a work order for the customer id in the body with no role check, and the security chain only requires sign-in for it.
